Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-11-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Jamie Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Luis Gomez (Redwood Product); Mark Reynolds (Sentinel CTO), Aisha Khan (ML Eng), Tom Lee (Platform), Kelly Moore (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Redwood walkthrough focused on edge cases: long-context workloads (~100k tokens/session), sustained high TPS (500-2k rps), streaming behavior causing backpressure/timeouts in customer infra. Discussed batching, KV cache, prefix caching, streaming windowing, autoscaling, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, and security considerations (VPC, KMS). Next steps: pricing, POC benchmark, security docs.

Topics: long context, high TPS, streaming backpressure, timeouts, API usage, Console demo, Redwood Optimize recommendations

Transcript:
[00:00] Jamie: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jamie Carter from Redwood, AE for NA. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Mark: Mark here, CTO at Sentinel. Aisha and Tom on too.
[00:11] Aisha: Aisha here.
[00:12] Tom: Tom, hi.
[00:13] Kelly: Kelly, SRE.
[00:15] Priya: Priya Nair, SE on the call, I'll run the deep dive demo.
[00:20] Jamie: Brilliant. We're going to walk through three parts: 1) API and Console quick tour, 2) Optimize recommendations for long context and high TPS, 3) a small live simulation showing streaming under load and how Redwood handles backpressure/timeouts. We'll leave time for Qs.
[00:35] Mark: Sounds good — our main pain is we have sessions that keep 80–120k tokens per user because we store long histories for enterprise search, and on peak we hit ~1.2k rps to the endpoint. We're seeing streaming clients get timeouts and on-prem proxies drop connections.
[00:50] Jamie: Got it. So long context + high sustained TPS + client streaming. Priya, quick thoughts?
[00:55] Priya: Yeah, so first, long context: Redwood supports models and serving configs that keep large KV caches and use optimized chunking. We do prefix+kv caching and sharded KV for big sequences. That said, in practice you want to avoid re-sending entire 100k on every request, so we recommend delta updates and pointer references, and our API supports partial context references.
[01:18] Aisha: When you say partial context references, do you mean we can reference stored blobs and only send pointers? Our security team frowns on leaving data outside their VPC.
[01:28] Priya: Right, good question. For Private or Dedicated you can host the store in your VPC and use signed pointer tokens. For Hosted we support encrypted pointer tokens too, but if you need full on-prem, we can run the private control plane. There's a bit of mis-match in the auto-transcript where it said "pointer tokens" as "point a tokens" earlier, ignore that.
[01:45] Tom: We're also concerned about the KV cache size — if you have 100k tokens per session, how does that affect per-GPU memory?
[01:52] Priya: So kernel selection and KV-eviction policies matter. We tested with 2xA100-80GB and 8xH100 configs; recommended approach is tiered caching, keep hot prefixes in fast GPU memory and cool ones in SSD-backed KV. The runtime can spill from GPU to NVMe and rehydrate on demand. That said, cold rehydration increases tail latency.
[02:18] Jamie: OK, that's the long-context side. Now on to high TPS and streaming backpressure. Priya, demo?
[02:25] Priya: Sure launching the Console — apologies if my screen is laggy, network is a bit flaky, sorry —
[02:30] [screen share starts — Console UI noise]
[02:33] Priya: Here's the per-route dashboard. You can see token cost, tail-latency percentiles, and active in-flight requests. For this customer pattern you want to configure autoscale pools with a predictable p99 latency SLO, but also set batching windows to avoid extreme fragmentation.
[02:50] Mark: Can you show where we set max in-flight per session? We had a bug where clients open multiple concurrent streams and we end up with head-of-line blocking.
[02:58] Priya: Yep, under Route config -> Advanced. You can set concurrency, per-session request limits, and enable prefix caching. Also you can enable streaming backpressure throttles — basically the server returns a 429-ish stream control header and the client SDK has hooks to backoff. I'll demo the SDK behavior in a sec.
[03:15] Aisha: Is that part of the hosted API or does that require Dedicated?
[03:19] Priya: Both. Hosted has sensible defaults; Dedicated gives you more control on kernel-level timeouts and autoscaler thresholds.
[03:24] [00:03:30] Luis: Quick note — Optimize can recommend batching windows given your sequence length distribution. You upload a small sample workload and Optimize returns configs.
[03:39] Tom: For our infra the main issue is streaming clients behind an on-prem proxy that times out after 30s; if the server stalls because of rehydration we get socket resets. Can Redwood stream partial tokens quickly so client sees progress?
[03:53] Priya: Yes we support immediate flush of prefix tokens and can do chunked streaming; we also have a streaming heartbeat to keep connections alive while long tail rehydrates. Heartbeat messages are not full tokens but keep proxies from closing. Note — some proxies choke on non-standard streaming frames, so we add compatibility modes (plain newline-separated data as a fallback).
[04:14] Mark: That compatibility mode sounds promising. Do you have customers using that with enterprise proxies?
[04:19] Priya: Yeah, we've seen it with financial customers; it reduces socket drops by about 70% in our internal tests, though there's a tradeoff with payload overhead.
[04:29] [04:30] Speaker 1 (transcription glitch): "We used the K V cash" — refers to KV cache — apologizing for the auto-text.
[04:35] Priya: No worries. Now I'll run a simulated load — small script that simulates 1k concurrent sessions, each doing a long-context continuation with streaming enabled. We'll watch the Console metrics (in-flight, queue length, kernel swaps).
[04:50] [05:00] (Simulated load starts)
[05:03] Priya: Ok load is up — you can see TPS ramping to ~1.1k rps, per-route p50~120ms, p95~340ms, p99 spikes around 1.6s initially as rehydration occurs. There's a brief backpressure event where queue length hits threshold and we start shedding to lower-tier capacity.
[05:28] Kelly: We see connections timing out at 30s on our side. How do you suggest we reduce the client-experienced timeouts?
[05:34] Priya: A few options: 1) enable streaming heartbeat so proxies see activity; 2) tune proxy timeouts (if possible) to be higher than your expected rehydration window; 3) use prefix-only responses initial flush to show partial results; 4) offload rehydration to a separate fast path — Redwood supports a prewarm API that warms KV for predicted sessions.
[05:58] Tom: Prewarm API — is that part of Dedicated or available in Hosted?
[06:03] Priya: Prewarm is available on Dedicated and as an enterprise add-on for Hosted; it requires provisioning a warm pool and some predict calls. It's costlier but reduces tail latency significantly.
[06:15] Mark: Cost question — if we go with Dedicated reserved capacity vs Hosted burstable, what's the rough unit economics for this workload?
[06:23] Jamie: I'll drop a simple matrix after this call, but short answer: Dedicated has higher fixed cost but lower per-token tail costs under sustained high TPS. Hosted is cheaper at baseline and for variable traffic, but if you're consistently at 1k+ rps, Dedicated typically reduces your total cost and gives deterministic SLOs. We'll send a modeled estimate for your traffic and token distribution.
[06:45] Aisha: Any notes on encryption and KMS when we reference pointer tokens? We need BYOK and HSM integration.
[06:52] Priya: We support customer-managed KMS and HSM for Private and Dedicated; for Hosted we have an envelope encryption model and can integrate with your key providers via secure connectors. We'll attach the security whitepaper and SOC2 artifacts.
[07:06] [07:10] (Sim results continued)
[07:12] Priya: You're seeing one of the timeout behaviors: when a kernel swap happens and NVMe rehydration is required, there's a few second hiccup. We mitigate with progressive flushing and heartbeat. Also Optimize recommends quantization for certain model layers to lower memory pressure. The Optimize UI will suggest a quantization profile — I'll show that.
[07:35] [screen: Optimize UI]
[07:38] Priya: Here Optimize ran an offline analysis on a sample of your sequences and recommended a mixed-quant profile: int8 for embeddings, bf16 for attention. It also recommended staggered batching windows — smaller batch size for interactive streams, larger batches for background bulk scoring. Note: automated suggestions are heuristics, we always run a POC to validate.
[07:59] Mark: Does quantization change correctness/quality for our summarization use case?
[08:04] Priya: Slight drop possible; Optimize scores quality regression against your eval set and flags regressions > threshold. You can also do per-route rollouts (canary) to watch quality metrics.
[08:16] Tom: For streaming, do you offer partial transcripts or token-level diffs so our UI can show progressive answer improvements rather than replacing the whole block?
[08:25] Priya: Yes the streaming SDK supports partial token deltas and patch-based updates. We also have structured output mode for JSON patches so your UI can merge without flicker. Some auto-transcription here wrote "json patch mode" as "Jason patch mode" earlier, ignore the name swap.
[08:42] Kelly: On observability — can we get trace ids from our side to Redwood logs so we can correlate?
[08:48] Priya: Absolutely, you can pass X-Trace-ID header and Redwood will include it in logs, traces, and Console traces. You can export to Datadog/Tempo via our trace forwarder.
[08:59] Aisha: We sometimes hit backpressure when multiple long sessions rehydrate concurrently, causing head-of-line blocking; would rate limiting per-session help?
[09:07] Priya: Yes per-session concurrency limits + per-route fair-queueing solves head-of-line. We also have a priority-tiering feature: critical sessions (e.g., live agent assist) get higher priority and preempt background scoring.
[09:20] [09:25] Mark: Any gotchas on scaling to 2k rps?
[09:28] Priia: Two things: kernel scheduling and NVMe bandwidth. At very high TPS with many long contexts, NVMe can be the bottleneck, so you either need more warm pool memory or faster NVMe (or different topology). We also recommend sharding by session prefix so hot sessions colocate.
[09:46] Jamie: Quick quick — can you summarize recommended configuration for Sentinel?
[09:50] Priya: Sure: Dedicated reserved capacity with warm pool, prewarm for top 5% of sessions, tiered KV (GPU hot + NVMe cold), streaming heartbeat and compatibility mode for your proxy, per-session concurrency limit = 2, route batching window 20ms for interactive, background scoring route with 200ms batching and larger batch sizes. Run POC with 2-week benchmark to validate tail p99 and cost.
[10:19] Mark: Sounds reasonable. What's the timeline to start a POC? We need internal approvals but ideally start early December.
[10:25] Jamie: We'll align — I'll send the pricing matrix and POC plan during EOD tomorrow. Priya will send the benchmark script.
[10:31] Tom: One more: what about endpoint failover if a region loses capacity? We need multi-region fallback for user-facing apps.
[10:36] Priya: Smart routing supports policy-based routing by latency/cost/region and automatic fallback to a compatible model variant. We can pin models for consistency. There is a small consistency tradeoff if you fallback to a lower-cap model, but we support automatic A/B rollback and dynamic model-switching.
[10:54] [11:00] (Documentation & links referenced)
[11:02] Jamie: I'll attach the links: pricing matrix doc, security.pdf, POC benchmark repo (link to gist), Optimize sample report.
[11:10] Aisha: Great. We'll review and try to get initial traffic patterns to you.
[11:13] Kelly: I'll coordinate with Tom to share proxy configs and timeout thresholds.
[11:16] Mark: Thanks everyone.
[11:18] Priya: Thanks all — quick recap in chat then I will stop the recording.
